lessons.title: Types of Charcoal Paper
lessons.body: Charcoal paper comes in three main types: laid, wove, and textured. Laid paper has parallel lines from the manufacturing process, giving a ribbed surface that grabs charcoal dust and creates a broken, linear texture. Wove paper is smoother and uniform, good for detailed work but holds less charcoal. Textured paper, often called 'tooth,' has a pronounced grain that catches charcoal particles, allowing for rich darks and expressive marks. In Africa, common brands include Canson Mi-Teintes (available in Nairobi, Lagos, and Johannesburg art shops), Fabriano Tiziano, and local alternatives like Kenyan-made 'Kraft' paper from Nairobi's Kamukunji market. For beginners, a pad of 130gsm (grams per square meter) charcoal paper is ideal. Lighter papers (90gsm) buckle when you apply wet media or heavy pressure. Heavier papers (160gsm and above) withstand erasing and blending. If you cannot find dedicated charcoal paper, try brown kraft paper (80-120gsm) from a packaging supplierâit has enough tooth for charcoal and is very cheap. Newsprint is another option but it is too smooth and tears easily; use it only for quick sketches. Always check the paper's surface: run your finger across it. If it feels like fine sandpaper, it will hold charcoal well. If it feels like glass, it will smudge and frustrate you. In West Africa, 'Sahara' brand charcoal paper is popular in Accra and Dakar. In East Africa, 'Canson' and 'Strathmore' are found in Kampala and Dar es Salaam. For a low-cost start, buy a roll of 'sugar paper' (also called kraft paper) from a stationery shop in your local market. Cut it to A3 size (297 x 420 mm) and tape it to a wooden board. This gives you a large, affordable surface to practice on. Remember: the paper you choose affects how your charcoal behaves. Soft charcoal on rough paper gives bold, grainy strokes; hard charcoal on smooth paper gives sharp, thin lines. Experiment with what you can find locally before ordering expensive imports.

lessons.title: Texture and Tooth
lessons.body: Texture and tooth are the two properties that determine how charcoal interacts with paper. Tooth is the microscopic roughness of the paper surfaceâthe peaks and valleys that catch charcoal particles. Texture is the visible pattern, like lines or bumps. A paper with high tooth holds more charcoal, allowing you to build deep blacks and soft gradients. A paper with low tooth (smooth) lets charcoal sit on the surface, making it easy to smudge but hard to layer. To test tooth, draw a single stroke with a soft charcoal stick (e.g., 6B or willow charcoal) across the paper. On high-tooth paper, the stroke will look broken and grainy. On low-tooth paper, it will be solid and dark. For African learners, common high-tooth papers include Canson Mi-Teintes (textured side), Fabriano Tiziano, and local 'rough' watercolor paper (300gsm). Low-tooth papers include Bristol board and smooth newsprint. The best paper for charcoal has medium toothâenough to hold layers but smooth enough for detail. You can create your own texture by sanding smooth paper with 120-grit sandpaper. Rub the sandpaper lightly over the surface in one direction, then the other, to create a cross-hatch tooth. This is a cheap way to turn cheap paper into charcoal-friendly paper. Another method: apply a coat of clear gesso or a mix of acrylic medium and fine sand (from a hardware store) to any paper. Let it dry, then draw. In Nigeria, artists often use 'Sahara' charcoal paper which has a natural tooth similar to Canson. In Kenya, 'Kraft' paper from Kamukunji has a rough side and a smooth sideâalways use the rough side for charcoal. When you blend charcoal with a tortillon or your finger, high-tooth paper will hold the blended tone, while smooth paper will just push the charcoal around. For a practice exercise, take three papers: newsprint (smooth), kraft (medium), and watercolor paper (rough). Draw the same simple shapeâa mango or a calabashâon each. Notice how the charcoal behaves differently. This will teach you to choose the right paper for the effect you want.

lessons.title: Toned Paper for Charcoal
lessons.body: Toned paper is any paper that is not whiteâusually grey, tan, blue, or ochre. Charcoal works beautifully on toned paper because you can use both black charcoal for darks and white chalk or white charcoal pencil for highlights. The paper's mid-tone acts as your middle value, saving time and creating a cohesive look. In Africa, you can find toned paper in art shops (Canson Mi-Teintes in 50+ colors) or make your own. To make toned paper cheaply, mix acrylic paint or gouache with water to a light wash, and brush it over a sheet of strong paper (e.g., 160gsm cartridge paper). Let it dry flat. Popular tones for African subjects: warm ochre (like the soil in Ghana), cool grey (like the sky in the Sahel), and terracotta (like the walls in Mali). For a portrait of a person with dark skin, a mid-grey or warm brown toned paper helps you render skin tones more realistically. You can also use brown kraft paper as a ready-made toned surfaceâit is already a warm tan. On toned paper, start with your darkest darks using compressed charcoal or a 6B stick. Then add white highlights with a white charcoal pencil (e.g., General's White Charcoal) or a piece of white chalk. The paper's tone becomes your mid-tone. This three-value system (dark, mid, light) is fast and effective. A common mistake is to cover the whole paper with charcoal, losing the tone. Instead, leave areas of the paper untouched to show the mid-tone. For a practice project, take a sheet of grey Canson paper (A4 size) and draw a simple still life: a banana, a tin cup, and a folded cloth. Use only black charcoal and white chalk. See how the grey paper unifies the drawing. In East Africa, 'Canson Mi-Teintes' in 'Felt Grey' or 'Tobacco' is popular. In West Africa, 'Sahara' toned paper in 'Sand' is common. If you cannot afford toned paper, buy a large sheet of brown kraft paper from a packaging shop and cut it to size. It costs a fraction of art paper and works well for charcoal studies.

lessons.title: Preparing Surfaces for Charcoal
lessons.body: Preparing your surface before drawing with charcoal is crucial for good results. First, choose a paper with enough tooth (see Lesson 2). If the paper is too smooth, you can roughen it with sandpaper (120-grit) or apply a coat of gesso mixed with fine sand. Second, tape your paper to a rigid boardâa piece of plywood or hardboard from a local carpenter works well. Use masking tape or brown paper tape. Tape all four edges to prevent curling. This also gives you a clean border. Third, if you plan to use wet media (like a charcoal wash with water), you must stretch the paper. Soak the paper in water for 5 minutes, lay it flat on a board, and tape the edges tightly. As it dries, it shrinks and becomes taut. This prevents buckling. For dry charcoal only, stretching is not necessary, but taping is still recommended. Fourth, consider applying a fixative before drawing? Noâfixative is used after drawing to prevent smudging. But you can apply a workable fixative between layers to build up darks without smudging previous layers. In Africa, local fixatives include cheap hairspray (unscented) or diluted PVA glue (1 part glue to 5 parts water) sprayed lightly. Test on a scrap first. Fifth, for a tinted ground, mix acrylic paint or gouache with water and brush it on. Let it dry completely before drawing. A common recipe: 1 part acrylic paint, 2 parts water. Apply with a wide brush in one direction, then dry. This gives a colored ground that shows through your charcoal. Sixth, if you are using charcoal powder, you can create a base tone by rubbing powder into the paper with a cloth. This is called a 'toned ground' and can speed up your work. Finally, always keep a scrap piece of the same paper nearby to test your charcoal strokes and values before committing to your final drawing. In Nigeria, artists often prepare kraft paper by sanding it lightly and wiping off dust. In Kenya, some use a mixture of cassava starch and water as a size to seal the paperâbut this can make it too smooth, so test first. Proper preparation saves you from frustration and wasted materials.

lessons.title: Testing Charcoal on Different Papers
lessons.body: Testing charcoal on different papers is the fastest way to learn which paper suits your style. You need at least four paper types: newsprint (smooth), cartridge paper (medium), kraft paper (rough), and watercolor paper (very rough). Also gather your charcoal: willow charcoal (soft, thin), compressed charcoal (hard, dark), and white charcoal pencil. For each paper, do the same set of tests. First, draw a single vertical line with willow charcoal, pressing lightly. Then draw another line pressing hard. Compare how dark each line is and how much texture shows. Second, make a gradient: start with heavy pressure at the top and gradually lift your hand as you move down. See how smoothly you can transition from dark to light. Third, try blending: use your finger or a tortillon to smudge a patch of charcoal. Note how easily it blends and whether it leaves a smooth or grainy finish. Fourth, test erasing: use a kneaded eraser to lift charcoal from a dark patch. High-tooth paper will leave a ghost image; smooth paper will erase almost completely. Fifth, test layering: draw a dark area, then try to add a lighter layer on top. On rough paper, layers build up; on smooth paper, they just mix. Record your results in a notebookâwrite the paper name and a few words about each test. In Africa, you can find these papers at local markets: newsprint from a newspaper printer, cartridge paper from a stationery shop, kraft paper from a packaging supplier, and watercolor paper from an art shop (or use the back of a calendar). For a cheap alternative to watercolor paper, use the rough side of a cement bag (washed and dried). After testing, you will know which paper to use for which effect. For example, if you want a detailed portrait, use cartridge paper. If you want a bold, expressive landscape, use kraft or watercolor paper. This knowledge will save you money and improve your drawings immediately. Do this test once a month with new papers you find.

lessons.title: Practice Project: Paper Comparison Study
lessons.body: For this project, you will create a single drawing that compares three different papers side by side. This will solidify your understanding of how paper affects charcoal. You need: three sheets of paper of the same size (A5 or 150 x 210 mm) but different texturesâe.g., smooth cartridge paper, medium kraft paper, and rough watercolor paper. Also, your charcoal set (willow, compressed, white pencil), a kneaded eraser, and masking tape. Tape each sheet to a separate board or to one large board with gaps between them. Choose a simple subject that has light, mid-tone, and dark areasâa ripe mango, a clay pot, or a folded headscarf. Draw the same subject on each paper using the same sequence: first, outline with willow charcoal. Second, block in the darkest shadows with compressed charcoal. Third, blend lightly with your finger. Fourth, add highlights with white charcoal pencil (if using toned paper) or erase out lights with a kneaded eraser (if using white paper). Fifth, refine edges and details. Work on all three simultaneously, spending about 20 minutes on each. This forces you to notice differences. After finishing, step back and compare. On smooth paper, your drawing will look sharp but may lack depth. On rough paper, it will look grainy and expressive but may lack detail. On medium paper, you get a balance. Write a short note on each drawing: 'Smooth: easy to smudge, hard to layer,' 'Rough: great texture, difficult for fine lines,' etc. Then, choose which paper you prefer for this subject and explain why in your notebook. For an African context, use locally available papers: a page from a cheap exercise book (smooth), a piece of brown kraft from the market (medium), and a sheet of rough watercolor paper or a washed cement bag (rough). If you cannot find white charcoal, use white chalk or even a piece of white soap (test first). This project takes about 2 hours. Repeat it with a different subject next week. Over time, you will develop a personal preference and a mental library of which paper to use for which effect. This is how professional artists in Lagos, Nairobi, and Accra make their choicesâthrough repeated testing.

quiz.q: Which type of charcoal paper has parallel lines from manufacturing?
quiz.explanation: Laid paper has a ribbed texture from parallel lines during production.

quiz.q: What is 'tooth' in the context of charcoal paper?
options: A) The color of the paper
B) The weight of the paper
C) The microscopic roughness that catches charcoal
quiz.explanation: Tooth refers to the surface roughness that holds charcoal particles.

quiz.q: Which paper weight is recommended for beginners to avoid buckling?
quiz.explanation: 130gsm is a good balance: heavy enough to resist buckling but affordable.

quiz.q: Which locally available paper is a cheap alternative for charcoal practice in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Brown kraft paper from packaging suppliers has enough tooth and is very cheap.

quiz.q: What happens when you draw on paper with low tooth?
options: A) Charcoal builds up in layers easily
B) The stroke looks broken and grainy
C) Charcoal sits on the surface and smudges easily
quiz.explanation: Low tooth means charcoal doesn't grip, so it sits on top and smudges.

quiz.q: How can you create tooth on smooth paper?
quiz.explanation: Light sanding creates a rough surface that holds charcoal.

quiz.q: What is a common brand of toned paper available in African art shops?
quiz.explanation: Canson Mi-Teintes is widely available and comes in many tones.

quiz.q: Why is toned paper useful for charcoal drawing?
options: A) It is cheaper than white paper
B) The mid-tone acts as a middle value, saving time
D) It glows in the dark
quiz.explanation: The paper's tone serves as the middle value, so you only add darks and lights.

quiz.q: Which color of toned paper is suggested for portraits of people with dark skin?
quiz.explanation: Mid-grey or warm brown tones help render skin tones more naturally.

quiz.q: What is a cheap way to make your own toned paper?
options: A) Use acrylic paint mixed with water as a wash
quiz.explanation: A diluted acrylic or gouache wash creates a colored ground.

quiz.q: Why should you tape your paper to a board before drawing?
options: B) To prevent curling and provide a clean border
quiz.explanation: Taping keeps the paper flat and gives a neat edge.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of stretching paper?
options: A) To make it dry faster
B) To prevent buckling when using wet media
C) To make it more absorbent
quiz.explanation: Stretching keeps paper taut and flat when it gets wet.

quiz.q: Which of these can be used as a local fixative in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Unscented hairspray works as a cheap fixative for charcoal.

quiz.q: What is a 'toned ground' in charcoal drawing?
options: A) A paper that is already colored
B) A base layer of charcoal powder rubbed into the paper
quiz.explanation: A toned ground is a layer of charcoal powder that creates a mid-tone base.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a scrap piece of the same paper nearby?
options: B) To test strokes and values before committing
quiz.explanation: Testing on scrap helps you avoid ruining your final drawing.

quiz.q: Which paper is best for detailed work?
quiz.explanation: Smooth paper allows for finer, more controlled lines.

quiz.q: What happens when you blend charcoal on high-tooth paper?
options: B) It holds the blended tone well
quiz.explanation: High tooth grips the charcoal, so blended tones stay in place.

quiz.q: Which test helps you compare how dark a charcoal line can get on different papers?
options: A) Drawing a single line with light and heavy pressure
quiz.explanation: Varying pressure shows the maximum darkness and texture of each paper.

quiz.q: What should you record when testing papers?
options: B) The paper name and observations about each test
quiz.explanation: Noting paper name and test results helps you remember which paper does what.

quiz.q: Which of these is a cheap alternative to watercolor paper for testing?
quiz.explanation: A washed and dried cement bag has a rough texture similar to watercolor paper.

quiz.q: In the paper comparison study, how many different papers should you use?
quiz.explanation: Three papers with different textures give a clear comparison.

quiz.q: What is the recommended subject for the comparison study?
options: B) A simple object with light, mid-tone, and dark areas
C) A landscape with many details
quiz.explanation: A simple object like a mango or clay pot allows you to focus on paper differences.

quiz.q: How long should you spend on each paper in the comparison study?
quiz.explanation: 20 minutes per paper is enough to see differences without fatigue.

quiz.q: What should you do after finishing the three drawings?
options: B) Write a short note on each about its characteristics
quiz.explanation: Noting observations helps you learn and remember.

quiz.q: Which paper is likely to give a grainy, expressive look?
quiz.explanation: Rough paper's texture creates a grainy, expressive mark.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when drawing on toned paper?
options: B) Covering the whole paper with charcoal, losing the tone
quiz.explanation: Covering the tone defeats the purpose of using toned paper.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended paper for charcoal?
quiz.explanation: Glossy photo paper has no tooth and repels charcoal.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a kneaded eraser in charcoal drawing?
options: B) To lift charcoal and create highlights
quiz.explanation: Kneaded erasers lift charcoal without damaging the paper.

quiz.q: Why is it important to test charcoal on different papers before a final drawing?
options: B) To know how the charcoal will behave and choose the right paper
D) To make the paper heavier
quiz.explanation: Testing prevents surprises and helps you select the best paper for your goal.

quiz.q: Which African city is mentioned as having art shops with charcoal paper?
quiz.explanation: Nairobi, Lagos, Johannesburg, Accra, Dakar, Kampala, and Dar es Salaam are mentioned.
